intro: Petroleum engineers analyze complex systems and make costly decisions, skills used across energy, environment and engineering management. The closest of the 25 careers below are Water Resource Specialists and biofuels product development managers, both at an 81% match, with medians of $167,220 and $171,270 for their broader BLS groups.
why_it_works: Planning a well means modeling rock and fluid behavior, evaluating risks and coordinating drilling teams on a tight budget. O*NET rates complex problem solving, judgment, systems analysis and systems evaluation at 3.88 out of 5 for this job. Water resources, brownfield work and geothermal production use the same expertise. Your pay is already high, so only 4 matches pay more. The gaps are operations and programming.
tips: Geothermal production management is a 72% match and uses your subsurface knowledge.
Computer and Information Systems Managers earn $175,140, which is 21% more, if you move toward data.
Learn programming for reservoir modeling; it is one of your main skill gaps.

faq.q: What jobs can former petroleum engineers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Water Resource Specialists (81%), biofuels product development managers (81%) and brownfield redevelopment specialists (77%), based on O*NET 31.0. Materials Scientists are 72% matched and earn $117,790, which is 19% less than the $144,910 petroleum engineer median.

faq.q: Which careers for petroleum engineers pay more?
faq.a: 4 of the 25 matches pay more than $144,910. Computer and Information Systems Managers earn $175,140 (21% more), Physicists $172,250 (19% more) and architectural and engineering managers $171,270 (18% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. Physics usually needs a graduate degree.

faq.q: Do petroleum engineers need another degree?
faq.a: Usually not. 21 of the 25 matches need no more education than petroleum engineers already have, including all of the top 10, while 4 usually need a graduate degree. A bachelor's degree is common, held by 50% of workers in the closest match.

faq.q: What skills should petroleum engineers learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are operations analysis, repairing, equipment maintenance and programming. Systems evaluation already rates 3.88 out of 5 for this job in O*NET, so software and operations skills are the main steps toward energy transition roles.
